name: Grief-focused therapy
heroTitle: Make room for the loss and the life that continues.
summary: Explore how grief-focused support can address loss, daily life, meaning, and connection without imposing a timetable or treating every grief experience as a disorder.
panelTitle: There is no required way to look bereaved.
panelParagraphs: Sadness, anger, numbness, relief, longing, and moments of enjoyment can coexist. Therapy should understand your experience rather than require a particular emotional performance.

model.title: Support does not require forgetting or moving on.
paragraphs: Grief-focused therapy can provide space to understand a loss and its effects on daily life, relationships, identity, and the future. The term covers different forms of support; it is not one universal protocol. The work should consider the nature of the loss, culture, relationships, circumstances, and the person's own goals.

Prolonged Grief Therapy is a specific treatment described by Columbia University's Center for Prolonged Grief. It is designed for a particular clinical difficulty involving persistent, impairing grief and focuses on adapting to loss while supporting restoration of life. That model should not be treated as evidence that ordinary bereavement is a disorder or that everyone needs the same treatment.

Grief support can make room for a continuing connection with what or whom was lost while addressing what life requires now. The task is not to erase memory, force acceptance on a deadline, or decide that feeling better betrays the relationship. Clinical assessment can help distinguish the support needed from a label chosen too quickly.

panel.title: Both loss and restoration can matter.
paragraphs: Talking about memories and facing practical demands are not competing loyalties. A person may need room for both, at different times and in different proportions.

example.title: Accepting an invitation feels like leaving someone behind.
example.intro: A fictional bereavement example about conflicting meanings, not a prescribed grieving task.

items.title: The invitation
paragraphs: A friend invites Lee to dinner several months after a loved one's death. Lee wants company but feels guilty at the thought of enjoying the evening.

items.title: The meaning
paragraphs: Enjoyment has become linked with the fear of forgetting or being disloyal. Staying home protects against that guilt but leaves Lee increasingly isolated.

items.title: The conversation
paragraphs: A therapist might explore what loyalty, memory, and connection mean to Lee, while considering whether social contact could coexist with grief rather than replace it.

reveal.title: What would a compassionate next step involve?
paragraphs: There is no single correct answer about the dinner. The work might clarify Lee's values, the meaning of the guilt, the support available, and what feels manageable. A choice could be small, reversible, and respectful of the relationship Lee wants to preserve in memory.

The example does not establish a diagnosis or a deadline for rejoining social life. The therapist should assess the actual person's functioning, distress, safety, and preferences rather than compare them with an ideal grieving schedule.

toolsTitle: Different parts of grief may need different kinds of attention.
toolsIntro: Open the cards to see why support can involve more than recounting the loss.

tools.title: The relationship and its meaning
tools.teaser: A loss is not defined only by an event date.
paragraphs: The relationship may have involved love, conflict, dependence, unfinished conversations, or mixed feelings. Grief can include meanings that are difficult to share with others.
A therapist should leave room for complexity rather than assume a uniformly positive relationship.

tools.title: Daily life and roles
tools.teaser: Practical changes can carry emotional weight.
paragraphs: Meals, finances, routines, parenting, and social contact may change after a loss. These tasks can bring reminders and new demands.
Practical support and emotional exploration can complement each other; not every difficulty is solved through insight alone.

tools.title: Memory and continuing connection
tools.teaser: Remembering does not have to prevent living.
paragraphs: Some people find meaning in memories, rituals, values, or forms of remembrance. The appropriate expression depends on the person and culture.
Therapy should not prescribe forgetting or force a ritual that feels wrong.

tools.title: When grief remains deeply impairing
tools.teaser: Specific treatment may be appropriate for some people.
paragraphs: A clinician can assess persistent distress and impairment and consider whether a specialized approach is indicated. Columbia's Prolonged Grief Therapy is one defined model, not a synonym for all grief counseling.
Assessment should also consider other mental health and safety needs.

processTitle: The work should follow the person, not a stage checklist.

process.title: Understand the loss
paragraphs: Discuss its meaning, circumstances, relationships, and current effects at a tolerable pace.

process.title: Clarify the need
paragraphs: Identify whether the priority is support, functioning, a specific clinical difficulty, or another concern.

process.title: Work with both grief and life
paragraphs: The plan may include emotional understanding, memories, practical adjustment, and reconnection, as appropriate.

process.title: Review without a deadline
paragraphs: Consider what is changing and what remains hard. Revisit the plan without requiring grief to disappear.

limitsTitle: A guide cannot decide whether your grief is ordinary or disordered.

limits.title: No universal timetable
paragraphs: Time since loss matters clinically, but it does not by itself determine a person's experience or the right support. Culture, circumstances, functioning, and symptoms all need consideration.

limits.title: Model-specific training is separate
paragraphs: A clinician offering grief support is not automatically trained in Prolonged Grief Therapy. Confirm the approach and scope rather than assuming a specific protocol from this page.

questions.question: Do I need to be ready to tell the whole story?
paragraphs: No. You can begin with what daily life is like or what you need help with. The clinician can explain how the work is paced and what information is needed.

questions.question: Will therapy make me stop missing the person?
paragraphs: That is not a reasonable promise. Support can focus on living with the loss, reducing impairment, and finding a workable relationship with memories and life now.

questions.question: What if my feelings are mixed?
paragraphs: Love, anger, relief, regret, and other feelings can coexist. A useful conversation does not require simplifying the relationship into one emotion.

questions.question: Is grief therapy only about death?
paragraphs: People seek support around different losses. The specific Prolonged Grief Therapy model discussed here concerns bereavement; its evidence should not automatically be generalized to every type of loss.

questions.question: When should I seek help?
paragraphs: You do not need to wait for a crisis to ask about support. Persistent difficulty functioning, severe distress, or safety concerns warrant an appropriate professional assessment. Urgent danger requires urgent help rather than an ordinary appointment inquiry.
